newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish Gdansk refinery in one-hour warning strike.
newsitem.headline: Polish Gdansk refinery in one-hour warning strike.

text.p: Some workers at Poland's Gdansk refinery staged a one-hour warning strike on Wednesday to demand free shares and a pay rise, a trade union official said.

"We do not want to whip up an atmosphere of a big strike. We only hang out flags and switched on syrens. Work was stopped only in auxiliray departments," Andrzej Cenacewicz, head of the Solidarity union in the refinery, told Reuters.

Four trade unions in the refinery, Poland's second largest, want a free 15 percent of shares in the company, in line with a privatisation bill passed last year. The law does not come into force until April 8.

"This issue cannot be discussed between the unions and the management. It is in the hands of the treasury minister and the government has to make a quick move," the president of the refinery, Wlodzimierz Dyrka, told a news conference.
Unions also demanded a 17-percent pay rise in 1997, a back pay increase for last year and a shorter working week.

"Considering the firm's financial situation the managemnt cannot fulfill the pay rise postulated in full. However, we will seek a compromise on wages as well as on the 40 hour working week," Dyrka said.
"At the current stage of investment, which we need to exist, cutting working hours is unacceptable," he added.
The warning strike came after a vote last week had shown the majority of workers supported strike action to press their demands.

The refinery is 75-percent owned by the state oil holding Nafta Polska SA with the remaining 25 percent directly controlled by the state. It processes about three million tonnes of crude oil annually.
"An escalation of the strike means the staff agrees it will be the end of the firm," the refinery's financial director Stanislaw Pokojski said.
